title: How Tardigrades Survive Drying Out
paragraphs: A square of moss on a north facing roof tile spends much of the summer as a brittle gray crust.
Crumble a pinch into a watch glass, add rainwater, and wait twenty minutes.
Under a dissecting scope the crust becomes a crowd.
Nothing in the dry crust looked alive.
Nothing in it was dead, either.
Tardigrades are a phylum of their own, mostly under half a millimeter long.
They live in ocean sediment, in soil, and in the thin films of water on moss and lichen.
A tardigrade is an aquatic animal.
It walks, feeds, and reproduces only while surrounded by water, and the water in a moss cushion is gone by noon.
The answer is cryptobiosis, from the Greek for hidden life.
A cryptobiotic animal is not dormant like a hibernating mammal: hibernation is a slowed metabolism, and cryptobiosis is, as far as any instrument can tell, no metabolism at all.
Biologists sort it by trigger: freezing gives cryobiosis, lack of oxygen gives anoxybiosis, and a sudden rise in outside salt gives osmobiosis.
Drying gives anhydrobiosis, the one the tardigrade performs best.
The change into the dried form, called a tun, is orderly and takes hours.
The animal pulls its head and legs inward, folds its cuticle into lengthwise creases, and contracts until its surface area drops by roughly half, slowing the escape of the water still inside.
Body water falls from about eighty percent of fresh mass to a few percent or less.
Measured metabolic rate falls below a hundredth of one percent of the active rate, below the detection limit of the instruments.
A tardigrade dried gradually, over several hours in fairly humid air, usually survives.
The same animal dropped into dry air and desiccated within minutes usually does not, because the tun is a program that needs time to run, not a passive collapse.
Ordinary drying wrecks an ordinary cell.
A phospholipid membrane holds its spacing because water molecules hydrogen bond to the lipid head groups.

Pull the water out and the heads crowd together, the sheet stiffens into a different phase, and when water is added back the membrane cracks along the boundaries between phases and leaks its contents.
The first molecule offered as an answer was trehalose, two glucose units joined head to head.

Because both anomeric carbons are tied up in that linkage, trehalose is nonreducing: it has no free aldehyde group waiting to react with the amino groups of nearby proteins, so it can be packed around delicate machinery at high concentration without browning it.
Under the water replacement idea, its hydroxyl groups take over the hydrogen bonds departing water leaves behind, propping membrane head groups apart near their normal spacing.

The second proposal is that trehalose turns the cell interior into a glass, not a windowpane but a physical state: a liquid dried or cooled so far past easy molecular motion that it seizes up without ever arranging itself into a crystal.
It has the disorder of a liquid and the rigidity of a solid.
Diffusion through it is slowed by many orders of magnitude, so two molecules that would ruin each other on contact never get far enough to meet.
A tun does not so much repair damage as refuse to let the reactions that cause it get started.
Trehalose, though, cannot carry the whole account.
Brine shrimp cysts and anhydrobiotic nematodes load themselves with the sugar, in some cases to a fifth of their dry weight.
Tardigrades accumulate far less, and in several species that dry and revive as reliably as any, trehalose is present only in traces or cannot be detected at all.
A molecule missing from an animal that performs the trick cannot be the whole explanation of the trick.
What fills the gap appears to be proteins that break the usual rule of one fold and one job.

Intrinsically disordered proteins have no stable fold, and they are promiscuous: rather than matching one partner the way a key matches one lock, they drape themselves over many different partners and take whatever form suits the one they meet.
Three families are abundant in tardigrades, named for where each sits: the cytoplasmic, secretory, and mitochondrial abundant heat soluble proteins.
They stay in solution when boiled, which is itself a signature of disorder.
As water leaves, the cytoplasmic family condenses into fibers and a gel that stiffens into the glassy state.
The clearest sign they do real work is that the trick travels.
Move the tardigrade genes for them into yeast or bacteria, organisms that ordinarily die when dried, and the engineered cells survive desiccation at rates their unmodified relatives do not.

Tardigrades carry a chromatin binding protein nicknamed the damage suppressor, which associates with DNA and appears to shield it from the hydroxyl radicals that radiation and oxidative stress generate.
When a tun takes up water it switches on a vigorous repair response, and part of what looks like invulnerability from outside is a first hour of frantic proofreading within.
Here the popular version drifts away from the biology.
Anhydrobiosis suspends metabolism, not chemistry, and certainly not time.
Inside a tun, slowly and without enzymes, oxygen still attacks lipids, sugars still condense onto proteins, and the DNA backbone still breaks.
The glass slows all of this by orders of magnitude.
It does not stop it.
The consequence is measurable: the longer a population stays dry, the smaller the fraction that walks away on rewetting, and the slower the survivors get moving.
Revival after several years in a dry moss sample is documented.
The much repeated figure of more than a century rests on one report that no one has reproduced, and it is better read as folklore than as data.
The rest of the folklore has the same shape: a real measurement with its conditions stripped off.
Tuns have been carried into low Earth orbit, exposed to vacuum and solar ultraviolet, and some came back.
Tuns have been held near absolute zero and above the boiling point of water, and some came back.
Both are true, and both describe a tun, briefly, with a survival fraction well short of everything.
The active, hydrated animal is not impressive at all.
Left in water a little above normal human body temperature it can die within a day.
Nothing in a tardigrade's history has ever asked it to survive orbit.
What its history asks, over and over, is that a film of water on a moss leaf vanish on Tuesday and return with Friday's rain.

The machinery that answers that, a cell interior converted into inert glass, is also indifferent to vacuum, cold, and much radiation, because all three do damage by moving molecules around and there are no molecules free to move.
The tardigrade is not built to be indestructible.
It is built to be dry, and indestructibility is a side effect.
That side effect is the part with an address in medicine.

Vaccines, antibody drugs, clotting factors, and living cells all depend on refrigeration, and the cold chain is expensive, power hungry, and the first thing to fail in a rural clinic or disaster zone.
A preparation that could sit on a shelf as dry powder and be revived with sterile water would change the logistics of global immunization.
The tardigrade suggests how to build one, and why the obvious attempt falls short.

Trehalose is already a common stabilizer in freeze dried products, but sugar alone gives a brittle glass that crystallizes over time or pulls moisture from the air and softens, and a softened glass lets molecules move again.
The lesson of the tun is that the sugar was never working alone.
Adding a tardigrade disordered protein to a human clotting factor preparation lets it be dried and rewetted with much of its activity intact.
The unsolved problems are the ones the animal faces too: the drying has to be slow and controlled, and anything thicker than half a millimeter dries from the outside in.
An organ is not a tun, and no one should promise that it will become one soon.
Back on the roof tile, the moss is gray again by afternoon.
The animals in it are not waiting, in any sense that involves an experience of waiting.
They are glass, and the glass keeps until the rain comes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the water content of a tardigrade in the tun state falls to
choices: a few percent of its fresh mass or less
one fifth of its fresh mass
less than a hundredth of one percent of its fresh mass
roughly half of its fresh mass
about eighty percent of its fresh mass

proof.quote: to a few percent or less

questions.why: Paragraph 4 gives the number outright: body water drops from about eighty percent of fresh mass to a few percent or less. The other figures in that same paragraph belong to different measurements, which is what makes this one worth reading slowly.
distractorNotes: A fifth of dry weight is the trehalose load of brine shrimp cysts in paragraph 8, a different animal and a different quantity.
Below a hundredth of one percent is the metabolic rate inside a tun, not its water content.
Roughly half is how much the animal's surface area shrinks, not how much water it keeps.
Eighty percent is the starting point, the water content of an active animal, not where it ends up.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that a tardigrade dried within minutes in very dry air usually dies because
choices: sudden drying tears the cuticle along its lengthwise creases
rapid water loss strips away the trehalose already stored in its tissues
tun formation is a program the animal needs hours to run
quick drying leaves too much water behind for a glass to form
the animal cannot take in enough oxygen while a tun is forming

proof.quote: the tun is a program that needs time to run

questions.why: Paragraph 4 sets the two schedules side by side. Dried gradually over several hours in humid air, the animal usually survives; dropped into dry air and desiccated in minutes, it usually does not, because the tun is a program that needs time to run rather than a passive collapse.
distractorNotes: Those creases are part of normal tun formation in paragraph 4, not a failure point the passage describes.
The passage never ties drying speed to trehalose loss, and paragraph 8 says several species get by with almost none of the sugar.
Leftover water is a problem for dried medical preparations in paragraph 16, not the reason fast drying kills the animal.
Oxygen supply is not the issue here; lack of oxygen appears in paragraph 3 only as a separate trigger, for anoxybiosis.

questions.stem: The passage says trehalose is nonreducing, and treats that as important because the sugar therefore
choices: can be stored at a fifth of the animal's total dry weight
has no free aldehyde group to react with protein amino groups
resists being broken down by the ordinary enzymes of the cell
arranges itself into a crystal as the last water is removed
cannot form hydrogen bonds with the head groups of a phospholipid membrane

proof.quote: no free aldehyde group waiting to react with the amino groups

questions.why: Paragraph 6 defines the term as it goes: both anomeric carbons are tied up in the linkage, so there is no free aldehyde waiting to react with the amino groups of nearby proteins. That is what lets the sugar be packed in at high concentration without browning the machinery it surrounds.
distractorNotes: A fifth of dry weight describes brine shrimp cysts in paragraph 8, and it is a quantity rather than a consequence of being nonreducing.
Enzyme resistance is never mentioned; the passage ties the nonreducing character to reactivity with proteins.
Paragraph 7 says the opposite, that the glassy state forms without ever arranging into a crystal.
This reverses paragraph 6, which says the sugar's hydroxyl groups take over exactly those hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: Which of the following does the passage offer as evidence that trehalose alone cannot account for tardigrade survival?
choices: Trehalose crystallizes inside a tun within a few years of drying
Some tardigrade species revive reliably with little or no detectable trehalose
Trehalose is absent from the dried cysts and seeds of every other organism studied
Tardigrades store more trehalose than brine shrimp cysts do
Trehalose cannot enter the cytoplasm until a tun has already formed

proof.quote: trehalose is present only in traces or cannot be detected at all
cannot be the whole explanation of the trick

questions.why: Paragraph 8 makes the argument directly. Brine shrimp cysts and anhydrobiotic nematodes load up on the sugar, tardigrades accumulate far less, and in several species that dry and revive as well as any, trehalose is present only in traces or cannot be found at all.
distractorNotes: Crystallizing sugar is a problem for dried medical formulations in paragraph 16, not something reported inside a tun.
The passage names two other organisms that are full of the sugar, so this is contradicted on the page.
Paragraph 8 says the reverse: the cysts load themselves with the sugar and tardigrades accumulate far less.
Nothing in the passage describes trehalose being kept out of the cytoplasm until a tun forms.

questions.stem: The protein nicknamed the damage suppressor is described as acting on
choices: DNA, by binding chromatin and shielding it
the trehalose stored in the cytoplasm
the phospholipids of the cell membrane
the repair enzymes switched on at rewetting
the folded shapes of the heat soluble proteins

proof.quote: which associates with DNA and appears to shield it

questions.why: Paragraph 11 introduces it as a chromatin binding protein that associates with DNA and appears to shield it from the hydroxyl radicals that radiation and oxidative stress generate.
distractorNotes: This protein binds DNA, and the passage never connects it to the sugar.
Membranes are handled by trehalose in paragraph 6, not by this protein.
Repair does switch on at rewetting in paragraph 11, but that is a separate response rather than what this protein binds.
The heat soluble families in paragraph 9 have no stable folded shape at all, and this protein is not described as acting on them.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 7, "glass" most nearly means
choices: a rigid solid state that keeps a liquid's disorder
a small vessel used for holding and viewing a specimen
a crystalline solid formed as the last water is removed
a thin protective coating laid down over a membrane
a hard, transparent material of the kind used in windows

proof.quote: the disorder of a liquid and the rigidity of a solid
without ever arranging itself into a crystal

questions.why: Paragraph 7 defines the word for the reader before using it: not a windowpane but a physical state, with the disorder of a liquid and the rigidity of a solid, in which diffusion is slowed by many orders of magnitude.
distractorNotes: A watch glass shows up in paragraph 1, but that is a piece of labware and has nothing to do with the state described here.
Paragraph 7 says the material seizes up without ever arranging itself into a crystal, so crystalline is the opposite of the sense meant.
Coating surfaces is what trehalose does in paragraph 6, while the glass is a state of the whole cell interior.
This is the everyday meaning, and the passage rules it out in the very sentence that introduces the term.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 9, "promiscuous" most nearly means
choices: changing chemically whenever the surrounding water leaves
moving freely between the cytoplasm and the mitochondria
present in unusually large amounts inside the cell
able to bind many different partners rather than one
reproducing without regard to a particular mate

proof.quote: they drape themselves over many different partners

questions.why: Paragraph 9 explains the word in the same sentence it appears: instead of matching one partner the way a key matches one lock, these proteins drape over many different partners and take whatever shape suits the one they meet.
distractorNotes: The proteins do condense on drying in paragraph 10, but that is a change of state, not what the word means here.
The three family names say where each protein sits, not that any of them travels between compartments.
Abundance is built into the family names in that paragraph, but it is a separate property from the binding behavior this word describes.
This is the everyday sense of the word, and the paragraph is describing molecular binding rather than mating.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which statement about a tardigrade while it is in the tun state?
choices: It repairs oxidative damage more slowly than an active animal does
It is chemically inert until water is added back to it
It loses the ability to revive at a steady, predictable rate
It accumulates damage that it cannot fix until water returns
It will survive indefinitely as long as it is kept dry

proof.quote: oxygen still attacks lipids
It does not stop it.
When a tun takes up water it switches on a vigorous repair response

questions.why: Two paragraphs combine here. Paragraph 12 says damage keeps building in the dry state even though metabolism is suspended, and paragraph 11 says the repair response switches on when a tun takes up water. So the fixing waits for rehydration.
distractorNotes: This assumes repair is still happening, only slower, but the passage places metabolism, and with it repair, at zero until water returns.
Paragraph 12 says the opposite: chemistry continues in the dry state even though metabolism does not.
Paragraph 12 says the surviving fraction falls the longer a sample stays dry, but it never claims the decline is steady or predictable.
Paragraph 12 rules this out, since survival drops with time dried and the century long claim is treated as folklore.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, a hydrated, active tardigrade exposed to radiation would most likely be
choices: less well protected than a tun, because its molecules are free to move
protected about as well as a tun, since the damage suppressor is always present
killed outright, since active animals carry no protective proteins
protected only if it had stored trehalose beforehand
unaffected, because radiation damage requires a dry cell interior

proof.quote: there are no molecules free to move
The active, hydrated animal is not impressive at all.

questions.why: Paragraph 14 gives the reason the tun shrugs off vacuum, cold, and much radiation: all three do their damage by moving molecules, and in a glass nothing is free to move. A hydrated animal has no glass, so that particular shield is missing.
distractorNotes: The damage suppressor does help, but paragraph 14 credits the broad tolerance to the glassy state, which a hydrated animal does not have.
This overshoots. Paragraph 11 describes DNA shielding in tardigrade cells without restricting it to tuns.
Trehalose belongs to the drying response, and paragraph 8 notes that some species manage with almost none of it.
Nothing ties radiation damage to dryness; paragraph 11 has radicals arising from radiation and oxidative stress generally.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central point of the passage?
choices: Tardigrades are the most durable animals known, and no laboratory has yet matched their tolerances
Surviving drying is a chemical strategy that slows damage rather than a form of invulnerability
Experiments in low Earth orbit have produced most of what is known about drying
The tardigrade genome should become the standard model for studying radiation damage
A single sugar, trehalose, accounts for the ability of small animals to survive without water

proof.quote: The tardigrade is not built to be indestructible.
indestructibility is a side effect
The glass slows all of this by orders of magnitude.
refuse to let the reactions that cause it get started

questions.why: The whole passage builds toward this. The tun works by turning the cell interior into a glass that keeps damaging reactions from getting started, which is a specific and limited trick, and paragraphs 15 and 16 argue that the trick, not toughness, is what dried medicines might borrow.
distractorNotes: Paragraphs 12 and 13 argue against this framing, calling the famous tolerances real measurements with their conditions stripped off.
Orbital exposure appears once, in paragraph 13, as an example of overstated folklore rather than as a main source of knowledge.
The passage never recommends a model organism, and radiation is a side topic inside the drying story.
Paragraph 8 takes this apart, since several species dry and revive with almost no detectable trehalose.

choices: establish trehalose as the central molecule of anhydrobiosis
argue that brine shrimp survive drying better than tardigrades do
compare the drying speed of tardigrades with that of nematodes
introduce the three families of heat soluble proteins by name
show that the leading single molecule explanation is incomplete

proof.quote: cannot carry the whole account
cannot be the whole explanation of the trick

questions.why: Paragraph 8 exists to open a gap. It grants that trehalose does real work in other animals, then points out that tardigrades carry far less and some carry none, which is exactly what makes the disordered proteins of paragraph 9 necessary.
distractorNotes: That is paragraph 6's job, and paragraph 8 pulls in the opposite direction.
The comparison is about how much sugar each organism stores, not about which one dries better.
Drying speed is a paragraph 4 topic and is not the comparison being drawn here.
The three families are named in paragraph 9, after this paragraph has cleared the ground for them.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the passage is organized?
choices: A medical problem, then a survey of the organisms that might solve it, then a proposed trial
A definition, then a debate between two research camps, then a verdict in favor of one camp
An observation, then its mechanism, then a correction of a popular overstatement, then a use for it
A popular claim, then the experiments that were said to confirm it, then a call for more study
A history of the field, then the single discovery that changed it, then the questions that remain open

proof.quote: Under a dissecting scope the crust becomes a crowd.
The answer is cryptobiosis
Here the popular version drifts away from the biology.
That side effect is the part with an address in medicine.

questions.why: The passage opens with moss on a roof tile, works through the tun, trehalose, the glassy state, and the disordered proteins, spends paragraphs 12 through 14 walking the indestructibility story back, and closes on dried medicines.
distractorNotes: The cold chain problem arrives late, in paragraph 15, rather than at the start, and no trial is proposed.
Trehalose and the disordered proteins are presented as partial and complementary answers, not as rival camps with a winner named.
The passage does the reverse of confirming the popular claim, and it ends with an application rather than a call for study.
There is no history of the field, and no single discovery is presented as the turning point.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the claim that tardigrades have revived after more than a century is best described as
choices: cautiously hopeful
angrily dismissive
openly admiring
plainly skeptical
entirely neutral

proof.quote: better read as folklore than as data
no one has reproduced

questions.why: Paragraph 12 grants that revival after several years is documented, then says the century long figure rests on one report nobody has reproduced and is better read as folklore than as data. That is doubt, stated calmly.
distractorNotes: Hope would suggest the author expects the claim to hold up, but the passage files it under folklore.
The tone stays measured, and the author faults the evidence rather than the people repeating the claim.
Admiration is not the note here; the author sets the claim aside rather than celebrating it.
Neutrality would mean reporting the claim without judging it, and the author judges it in the same sentence.

questions.stem: In discussing what the tardigrade's chemistry might do for medicine, the author's stance is best described as
choices: doubtful that dried preparations will ever be more than a curiosity
indifferent to whether the approach ever reaches patients
interested in the approach and candid about its limits
convinced that room temperature storage of tissue is close at hand
impatient with researchers who have failed to solve the problem

proof.quote: would change the logistics of global immunization
no one should promise that it will become one soon

questions.why: Paragraph 16 treats the sugar plus protein route as worth building on, reports a clotting factor dried and rewetted with much of its activity intact, then lists what is unsolved and ends by saying an organ is not a tun and nobody should promise that it will be one soon.
distractorNotes: Doubt that deep does not fit a paragraph reporting a clotting factor dried and rewetted with much of its activity intact.
Paragraph 15 spends its length on rural clinics and disaster zones, which shows the author cares about reaching patients.
The closing sentence of paragraph 16 refuses exactly this optimism about anything thicker than half a millimeter.
No blame is placed on researchers; the obstacles are described as the same ones the animal itself faces.

questions.stem: The passage supports all of the following statements EXCEPT:
choices: Some tuns have survived exposure to the vacuum of low Earth orbit
An active tardigrade can be killed by water a little warmer than the human body
Certain tardigrade species contain little or no detectable trehalose
Yeast or bacteria given tardigrade genes can survive drying better than usual
A tun protects itself by running its metabolism at a low but steady rate

proof.quote: exposed to vacuum and solar ultraviolet, and some came back
it can die within a day
trehalose is present only in traces or cannot be detected at all
the engineered cells survive desiccation at rates their unmodified relatives do not
no metabolism at all
below the detection limit of the instruments

questions.why: Paragraphs 3 and 12 are explicit that cryptobiosis is no measurable metabolism at all rather than a slowed one, and paragraph 7 credits the protection to a glass that keeps reactions from starting. Each of the other four statements sits on the page.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 13 reports tuns carried into low Earth orbit and exposed to vacuum, with some coming back.
Paragraph 13 says a hydrated animal left in water a little above normal body temperature can die within a day.
Paragraph 8 says trehalose is present only in traces, or not detectable at all, in several reliable species.
Paragraph 10 says engineered yeast and bacteria survive desiccation at rates their unmodified relatives do not.

questions.stem: A reader looking for the physical reason a dried membrane leaks when water is added back to it should turn to
choices: paragraph 3
paragraph 14
paragraph 7
paragraph 11
paragraph 5

proof.quote: the membrane cracks along the boundaries between phases and leaks its contents

questions.why: Paragraph 5 walks through the whole sequence: water normally hydrogen bonds to the lipid head groups, removing it lets the heads crowd together and the sheet shift phase, and on rewetting the membrane cracks at the phase boundaries and leaks.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 3 defines cryptobiosis and its varieties without touching membranes.
Paragraph 14 argues that the extreme tolerances are a side effect of drying, with no membrane detail.
Paragraph 7 describes the glassy state, which concerns diffusion through the cell interior rather than membrane structure.
Paragraph 11 is about DNA shielding and the repair response at rewetting.

questions.stem: A laboratory wants to store a fragile protein drug as a dry powder that stays active for months on a shelf. Based on the passage, which preparation is most likely to succeed?
choices: trehalose alone, dried in minutes as a thin film
trehalose alone, dried slowly into a thick block
trehalose and a disordered protein, dried slowly as a thin film
the damage suppressor protein alone, dried in minutes as a thick block
a disordered protein alone, dried slowly into a thick block

proof.quote: sugar alone gives a brittle glass that crystallizes over time or pulls moisture from the air and softens
Adding a tardigrade disordered protein to a human clotting factor preparation lets it be dried and rewetted with much of its activity intact
the drying has to be slow and controlled, and anything thicker than half a millimeter dries from the outside in

questions.why: Paragraph 16 hands you the recipe and its limits. Sugar alone gives a glass that crystallizes or softens with time, a disordered protein added alongside the sugar keeps a dried protein active, and the drying has to be slow and no thicker than half a millimeter. Only one preparation respects all three.
distractorNotes: Sugar alone is the obvious attempt paragraph 16 says falls short, and drying in minutes breaks the slow and controlled rule in the same paragraph.
Slow drying is right, but sugar alone still crystallizes or softens with time, and anything thicker than half a millimeter dries from the outside in.
The damage suppressor shields DNA in paragraph 11 and is never offered as a glass former, and a thick block dried in minutes breaks both drying rules in paragraph 16.
The protein is the right ingredient, but paragraph 16 says anything thicker than half a millimeter dries from the outside in, so the block is the problem.
